subject: how-banks-work
title: Where Does Bank Money Go?
summary: Your bank money doesn't sit in a vault. Here's where it goes, how banks earn money, and what keeps it safe.

keys.prompt: Where is most of the money people put in a bank?
keys.answer: It is lent out to people and businesses who borrow it. The bank keeps only part of it as cash.

options.text: Lent out to people and businesses
Locked in a vault with each person's name
Sent to the government to keep

keys.prompt: How does a bank make money from lending?
keys.answer: It charges borrowers more interest than it pays savers. The bank keeps the difference.

options.text: It charges borrowers more interest than it pays savers
It keeps money that savers forget about

keys.answer: It protects money in accounts at insured banks, up to $250,000 for each person at each bank, if the bank fails.

options.text: Protects bank account money if the bank fails
Makes the bank pay you more interest
Protects money you put in stocks

cards.title: Picture a giant vault
cards.text: Say you put $20 in a bank. You might picture it in a big vault with your name on it. But that is not what happens. So where does it go?

cards.question: Where do you think most of the money in a bank is right now?

options.text: Lent out to people and businesses
Sent to the government to keep

cards.reveal: Most of it is lent out! A bank keeps only part of its money as cash. It lends the rest to people and businesses.

cards.title: Your money goes to work
cards.text: A bank puts together money from lots of savers. It keeps only part of it as cash. It lends the rest to people who need to borrow. A family might borrow to buy a home. A business might borrow to buy new machines.
cards.example: Say a bakery borrows money from the bank to buy a new oven. Some of that money might be yours!

why.q: Why doesn't the bank just keep all the money in the vault?
why.a: Lending is how the bank earns money. People who borrow have to pay back extra, called interest.

cards.title: The interest gap
cards.text: When you save, the bank pays you a little extra. That extra is called interest. When people borrow, they pay the bank more interest than the bank pays savers. The bank keeps the difference.
cards.example: Say you save $100 and the bank pays you $2 in a year. It lends that $100 to a bakery, and the bakery pays $7. The bank keeps $5.

cards.title: Not everyone at once
cards.text: Banks count on one simple thing. On most days, only a few people take their money out. So the bank only needs a little cash on hand. But what if lots of people came at the same time?

cards.title: A bank run
cards.text: When lots of people rush to take out their money at once, it's called a bank run. The bank can't pay everyone right away, because most of the money is lent out. In the early 1930s, waves of bank runs hit the United States.

why.q: Why would people rush to the bank just because others are?
why.a: Each person worries the cash will run out before they get theirs. So people rush, and that can make a bank fail.

cards.title: A safety net
cards.text: In 1933, Congress created the FDIC. It protects money in accounts at insured banks, up to $250,000 for each person at each bank. Since then, no one has lost a penny of insured money. So people have less reason to rush.
cards.example: Banks pay for this insurance. It covers money in checking and savings accounts, but not stocks.

cards.question: If you ran a bank, how would you decide who to lend money to?
nudges: What would you want to know about the person or business first?
What could go wrong if they couldn't pay you back?

questions.q: Where is most of the money people put in a bank?

options.text: Lent out to people and businesses
options.why: Yes! The bank keeps only part of it as cash.

options.text: In a vault with each person's name
options.why: That's what many people picture. But most of it is lent out.
No. The bank lends most of it to people and businesses.

questions.q: A bank pays savers $2 and gets $7 from a borrower. What does the bank keep?

options.why: Right! $7 minus $2 is $5. That gap is how the bank earns money.
The bank pays the $2 out to savers, so it subtracts. $7 minus $2 is $5.
The $2 goes to the saver. The bank keeps what's left: $5.

questions.q: Why does FDIC insurance make bank runs less likely?

options.text: Insured money is safe even if the bank fails
options.why: Yes! So there's no reason to rush to beat everyone else.
No. It protects the money, so people don't need to rush in.

options.text: It makes banks keep all the cash in a vault
options.why: Banks still lend most of it. The insurance protects the money instead.

sources.title: Understanding Deposit Insurance
sources.supports: The FDIC was created by Congress and founded in 1933; since then no depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds; deposits are insured to at least $250,000 per depositor, per ownership category, at each FDIC-insured bank; insurance premiums are paid by FDIC-insured banks; it covers checking and savings accounts but not stock investments.

sources.title: Bank run
sources.supports: Banks keep only a fraction of deposits as cash and lend the rest; banks pool many deposits into loans for businesses and households buying homes and cars; banks charge much higher interest on loans than they pay on deposits, which earns a profit; on any one day only a small share of accounts is withdrawn; a bank run is when many people withdraw at once; once a run starts it is rational to join it, and runs can make a bank fail; the Great Depression had runs on many banks from 1929 to 1933; deposit insurance removes the incentive to withdraw just because others are.
